# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.

- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why5: The scale is mine, but the belief adds 'with hearing aids or phone captions', which narrows today's way to two tools when many of my people also lipread, ask for repeats or just nod along.
screens.why7: One measure (how much of the talk was followed), five rungs best to worst, the first working, the last failing outright, the line under a working rung so the belief can be supported or refuted, and the act (following a conversation) takes the I can't recall escape.
screens.instead: Keep the five, and have the belief say 'following what was said, the way they manage today, still falls short' rather than naming only hearing aids or phone captions.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the problem screens are checked.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the pick 'Lock and record the face Keel preselects' needs a second read: 'lock' and 'preselects' are Keel's words, not mine.
screens.why3: I know my respondents are deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, so I can judge from my own life how they should be asked.
screens.why4: The face options are fine, but for my people the true answer is missing: no text-first or captioned-video option without a spoken interviewer, and no signing (ASL) interviewer for Deaf respondents. The hint's note that questions are written on screen only half covers this.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks to the respondent, and the screen keeps what I set up.
screens.instead: How should people meet your questions? (Captions on video with the AI interviewer / Text only, read and tap / An interviewer who signs in ASL, with captions)

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, picking how my respondents answer is the obvious next step before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Each option is short and concrete, and for my audience the line that every question is also written on the screen is exactly what I need to see.
screens.why3: I know my users well enough to pick this myself: many deaf and hard-of-hearing adults would rather read than listen to a voice on video, so I chose Read and tap.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real choices, including letting people choose, and my pick, Read and tap, is there with a typing route for anyone who doesn't speak.
screens.why5: It names my respondents in my own words, deaf or hard-of-hearing adults, and nothing about the glasses or the pricing shows through.

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how people answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious next step before anything is sent.
screens.why2: The first and third options are in my voice ('I send', 'I post'), but the second switches to 'you send them' and names a 'Contacts page' I haven't seen yet in this flow, so I read it twice.
screens.why3: I know who I'd reach: wearers I've met through TranscribeGlass, people from HLAA chapters, and deaf and hard-of-hearing Facebook groups, so I can answer at once.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I'd actually reach people (named contacts, a found list, or one link posted in a community group), and my pick is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps' product or roles is on this screen, and my answer 'People I know by name' stands as I picked it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People I find with Keel (I pick a list from Keel's search; Keel makes a link for each and I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post one link where they already gather; each signs in with Google, then is interviewed)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' is up top, but the number beside it, median 4 days, sits inside my 4-to-7 range and reads like a pass; the deciding count (4 of 7 at or beyond, bar 5, 1 short) is only down in the Frequency card.
screens.why_b2: There's no chart, just a tally and per-card counts with bars; Prevalence, Importance and Current solution read fine, but the Frequency card stacks a split line, median, below, at-or-beyond and bar into one dense run, and Importance prints '7 of 7 put it in their two' twice, so I had to read them twice.
screens.why_b3: The four dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, with my 8 in 10, my 4 to 7 days, hearing aids and phone captions; Importance's 'have three things that are hard' is clunky but is still my belief.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what a 4-versus-3 split on frequency means for AirCaps, for example whether the wedge should be people who face this daily or whether 2 to 3 days a week still justifies $599 glasses.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown everywhere and nothing is called strong, but no line says that 7 people is a small sample, and three 'Holding up' calls on 7 answers carry more weight than they should without that caveat.
screens.instead: Lead with 'Frequency is split: 4 of 7 lose the thread on 4+ days a week, you needed 5 of 7, so 1 short', say that 7 answers is a small sample, and add a line on what to do, e.g. narrow the wedge to people in daily group settings or test whether 2 to 3 days a week is enough to buy glasses.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding numbers, '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven 'for' cells on a 0 to 7 axis with my marker at 6, so I see at first look what is counted (yes at the gate), over how many (7) and where my bar sits.
screens.why_b3: The card is Prevalence and the event 'lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people' is mine, but the belief says 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' and drops the segment I typed: in the US, talking with hearing people every week.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7' tells me the problem is widespread enough, and it points me to Frequency and Importance next, which is where the stage page says people disagree.
screens.why_b5: n is on the screen ('7 answered · 7 counted') and the small group is named outright ('a lean, not a call'), so a clean 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: At least 8 in 10 deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people in the last 7 days. Also drop the stray '— the most recent time it happened' after the gate question.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits right beside 4 of 7 at or beyond my 4 days against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts days out of 7 over 7 people, but it draws a 0 tick nobody could pick, and "bar" means two things here: my 4-to-7 band in the bar line and 5 of 7 people on the strip. The legend's "at what you said" also doesn't match the list's "inside what you said", so I needed a second look.
screens.why_b3: It is my Frequency belief in my words: deaf and hard-of-hearing adults losing the thread of a conversation with hearing people on 4 to 7 days out of 7.
screens.why_b4: "Whether it matters is the next card" sends me elsewhere instead of saying what a 4-against-3 split means for me, for example whether to aim at the people who hit this most days or move my claim down to 2 to 3 days.
screens.why_b5: The low n is stated plainly ("a lean, not a call"), but the Asked line ends with "the most recent time it happened", which misdescribes a question that asked for a count of days.
screens.instead: Drop "the most recent time it happened" from the Asked line, start the ticks at 1, and say: 4 of 7 lost the thread on 4+ days and 3 on fewer, 1 short of the bar; consider leading with the people who hit this most days, or claim 2 to 7.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by what number.
screens.why_b2: The bar and the 7 people are plain, but the caption says each picked two while the bars add to 11, not 14, and I had to work out that three stopped at Nothing else.
screens.why_b3: Importance is my dimension, but the own row reads as following what hearing people are saying, a narrowing of my job to follow and join a face-to-face conversation, so it is recognisable rather than my exact words.
screens.why_b4: The So line rightly says top two, not first, but it never says what that means for caption glasses, such as that the core pain is confirmed and joining in is the next pain to weigh.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called a lean, not a call, and the claim stays inside these 7.
screens.instead: 7 of 7 put following the talk in their two, and 3 stopped there; getting a word in came second (3), so the glasses should help me join in, not just read along.

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it, and they agree.
screens.why_b2: Each of my five rungs has its count, my line sits under 'Missed only a little', and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against, with the marker at 5 of 7, so what's counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The card is Current solution, the rungs are the ones I saved word for word, and the belief line ('following what was said with hearing aids or phone captions still falls short') is my act and my belief; the only rewording is 'face-to-face conversation' in the stem where I'd have said group conversation.
screens.why_b4: 'Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study' tells me to move on, but not what the gap means for the glasses, e.g. that everyone short of the line still caught the gist or more and nobody lost it entirely, so the captions have to beat partial following, not silence.
screens.why_b5: It keeps to 'these 7', says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and shows Tomás's quote and his count against, so nothing claims more than seven people can carry.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of these 7: 3 caught only the gist, 3 missed most of it, and nobody lost it entirely, so the glasses must beat 'getting the gist' in groups and noise; a small group, so read it as a lean before the solution study.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Holding up' with '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7' right beside it, so I see the verdict and the deciding number together.
screens.why_b3: 'Current solution' and the belief about hearing aids or phone captions still falling short are the dimension and the line I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what the held line or Tomás's workaround means for the idea, and the 'When a line fails' heading sits over a line that held, with no next step under it.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 of 7, 1 against, 1 asked here), and the single quote is shown as one person ('On their own (1)') and not made into a trend.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's end-seat trick for one-sided deafness is something I did not type: it suggests people with single-sided loss manage well enough without the glasses and are a weaker part of my wedge.
screens.instead: Current solution held 6 of 7; the one who manages today is deaf on one side and fixes it by choosing a seat, so lead with people who have loss in both ears. Frequency split 4 to 3 with no why asked, so ask how many days a week the hard conversations come before you plan around daily wear.

screens.why1: As the opening screener it plainly checks whether I'm someone this study is about, and I am: I talk with hearing people at work and at the shops every week.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how I and everyone I know say it, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: It asks about my own week, and I know without thinking that yes, I do.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate like this, and no escape is right for a screener.
screens.why5: Nothing of any product leaks, but it drops "face to face" and turns the last 7 days into a habit ("every week") even though the kicker says "A recent time", so it has drifted a little from the founder's situation.
screens.why6: It is easy to hear, but "I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No." is a clumsy way to offer a yes-or-no question, where the guidelines say a screener should just end with "Yes or no."
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, asking if I lost the thread with them this week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Losing the thread is exactly how I would say it when I can't keep up with hearing people talking.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost track of a conversation in the last week; it happens to me, I don't have to guess.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and the chips only show up after a Yes for the story, so they don't muddle the gate.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but it dropped face to face and the too fast or too noisy part, so a phone or video call slip could count.
screens.why6: One short sentence, then yes or no; easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate is two fixed answers with no escape and a No is truly possible, but face to face is dropped from the founder's segment, so the event drifts a little.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose the thread of a face-to-face conversation with hearing people? Yes or No.

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, I lost the thread this week, it makes sense to ask how many days that happened.
screens.why2: Losing the thread is exactly how I'd put it when a conversation with hearing people runs away from me, and 'how many of the last 7 days' is clear on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know which days I had to bluff or ask someone to repeat at work, at the shop or with family, so I can count them.
screens.why4: One button for each day from 1 to 7 covers every true answer after a yes, with no zero and no overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits if the week blurs together.
screens.why5: It asks only about my own conversations in plain words, and nothing about a product, captions or a company reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with 'say a number from 1 to 7' and one escape, easy to hold, though I'd want it on screen too because I'm hearing it.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of days in the window, from 1 to 7 in order with no zero; the window's unit is said once, the event is a single act on a given day, and the one 'I can't recall' escape is there; the balance depends on the founder's low, which I can't see.

screens.why1: Right after asking how often I lost the thread, it makes sense to ask which part of talking with hearing people I'd most want made easier.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but 'a seat where they can see every face' made me stop, because the seat is for me, so I'd expect 'where you can see' or 'where I can see'.
screens.why3: I just had a conversation like that, and I know which of these was hard for me.
screens.why4: Choosing a seat is how I manage to follow the talk, so it overlaps with 'following what hearing people are saying', and the list leaves out things I really do, like getting people to repeat themselves or face me.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product reaches me, but the seat row's 'they' sounds like it was written about deaf people rather than to me, so it drifted a little.
screens.why6: One short question and three short options read as a list, with one escape at the end, so I can hold it and answer by ear.
screens.why7: The own item, following what hearing people are saying, is there, not first, and can be picked or passed over, and None of these is at the first ask; but the seat row is a means of the own row that the card says should be put aside, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Following what hearing people are saying · Getting a word in at the right moment · Getting people to repeat what you missed · None of these

screens.why1: After asking which part I'd most like easier, it makes sense to ask how my last conversation actually went with what I use now.
screens.why2: Most of the words are mine, but 'hearing aids or phone captions' puts two tools in one breath, so I have to stop and work out which one it means. It also says 'face-to-face conversation' where the earlier screens said 'with hearing people'.
screens.why3: I can answer how much I followed, but if I lip-read, used my implant, or had nothing at all that day, the stem doesn't describe my conversation and I'd be guessing.
screens.why4: The five run cleanly from everything to nothing without overlapping, in words I'd use myself. 'I can't recall' fits, because nobody else can follow a conversation for me.
screens.why5: Hearing aids and phone captions are what people like me really use today, and nothing about a new product or the company's own terms reaches me.
screens.why6: The options are short and easy to hold, but 'following what was said with hearing aids or phone captions' is a long clause with an 'or' in it to keep in my head before the list starts.
screens.why7: The five are one ladder of how much was followed, with a working rung first, total failure last and the right escape, but the stem pastes a tool list onto the act, which the card names as a pitfall.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of what was said did you follow? Followed everything that was said; Missed only a little; Caught only the gist; Missed most of it; Could not follow it at all — or I can't recall.
